alignment.note: ὁ / ܗܘ / ille — anaphoric subject pronoun.

The postpositive Greek δέ and its Syriac calque ܕܝܢ stand in second position, whereas the Latin renders the adversative connective with At in initial position; the placement difference is purely a feature of the receiving languages' particle syntax and carries no semantic weight.

Greek uses the aorist passive participle ἀποκριθείς ('having answered') in a periphrastic 'answered and said' Semitism; Syriac ܥܢܐ is a finite verb coordinated with the following ܘܐܡܪ, while Latin respondens preserves the participial construction — all three reflect the same underlying Semitic idiom realised by differing grammatical means.

Greek has a single finite verb ἔφη ('he said'); the Peshitta supplies the conjoined finite verb ܘܐܡܪ ('and said') to complete its 'answered and said' pairing, whereas the Latin ait stands alone matching the Greek single-verb pattern.

The Clementine Vulgate inserts an explicit colon before the vocative to mark the onset of direct speech; neither the Greek nor the Syriac transmits a discrete punctuation token here, the speech boundary being conveyed lexically.

The Greek middle aorist ἐφυλαξάμην ('I kept for myself') connotes a reflexive nuance of self-interested observance; both the Syriac ܢܛܪܬ and the Latin observavi render a plain active 'I kept/observed,' losing the middle-voice colouring that the Greek attaches to law-keeping here.
Syriac supplies an explicit feminine-plural pronominal object ܐܢܝܢ ('them') resuming ܟܠܗܝܢ, a typical Aramaic resumptive object-marker; Greek and Latin leave the object unexpressed within the verb.

Greek and Latin express the possessive analytically with noun plus genitive pronoun (νεότητός μου / juventute mea), whereas Syriac compresses the phrase into a single word ܛܠܝܘܬܝ bearing a suffixed first-person possessive ('my youth'), a synthetic morphological strategy equivalent in sense.
